headline: Nine Indian-American Republicans on the Ballot as the GOP Turns Against H-1B Visas
subheadline: At least nine Indian-American Republicans contest the November 3 elections — even as their party's leadership pushes the toughest crackdown on skilled-worker immigration in decades.
body:
• At least nine Indian-American Republicans are on the November 3 ballot — led by Vivek Ramaswamy's toss-up Ohio governor bid — even as their party's leadership pushes the toughest crackdown on skilled-worker immigration in decades.
  • On October 8, Vice President JD Vance said the United States should welcome only workers with "truly elite specialized skills"; House Republicans have introduced a bill with fines of up to $250,000 per H-1B violation and 10-year bans for violators.
  • What this means for you: the $100,000 H-1B petition fee remains blocked by two federal court orders, and the October 8 PERM suspension covers green-card processing at Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCLTech and Capgemini — if your case sits with one of those employers, check its status with your company's immigration counsel.
  • Polling shows the backlash is costing the GOP: 66% of Indian Americans oppose the $100,000 fee (Carnegie 2026), and Trump's support among Indian-American men aged 18–39 has fallen from 40% in 2024 to 24%.

Nine Indian-American Republicans are contesting the November 3 elections across the United States — running for governor, attorney general and Congress — at the exact moment their own party has turned the H-1B visa programme into its favourite punching bag. The contradiction was on full display this week, as the Trump administration rolled out a fresh round of restrictions on skilled-worker immigration while Indian-American candidates knocked on doors in some of the cycle's most watched races.

A week of escalation

The latest wave began on October 8, when Vice President JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspension of the Labor Department's PERM green-card programme for eight firms — Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCLTech and Capgemini. At the same press conference, Vance said that "most H-1Bs" are used to replace American middle-class workers and that the country should welcome only people with "truly elite specialized skills," according to Reuters. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the action sends "a strong signal to every single employer."

Two days earlier, House Republicans introduced the H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act, which would impose fines of up to $250,000 — about ₹2.4 crore — per violation, 10-year bans for offending employers and $50,000 fines for document fraud, Gulte reported. The administration's separate $100,000 fee on certain H-1B petitions has now been blocked by a second federal judge, with the government separately pursuing a permanent fee of roughly $103,000.

"Most H-1Bs are used to replace American middle-class workers. We should welcome only people with truly elite specialized skills."

— Vice President JD Vance, October 8 press conference

The candidates caught in the middle

The timing could hardly be worse for the party's Indian-American standard-bearers. Vivek Ramaswamy's bid for Ohio governor — rated a toss-up by all three major forecasters, with Democrat Amy Acton ahead by 4.6 to 4.8 points in polling averages — is the marquee race. In New York, Trump-endorsed Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal judge nominee, is challenging Attorney General Letitia James, who led 52–39 in a September Siena poll.

Three Indian-American House candidates face long odds in Democratic seats: Ritesh Tandon against Ro Khanna in California's 17th, Nirav Sheth — who came to the US as an engineering student in 2008 and served in the Marine Corps — against Pramila Jayapal in Washington's 7th, and Mahesh "Max" Ganorkar against Valerie Foushee in North Carolina's 4th. IANS reported that at least nine Indian-American Republicans are on ballots nationwide.

The diaspora pushes back

The numbers suggest the party's immigration hard line is alienating the very community these candidates represent. The Carnegie 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey found 66% oppose the $100,000 H-1B fee, 71% disapprove of Trump's first-year performance, and Trump's support among Indian-American men aged 18–39 has collapsed from 40% in 2024 to 24%. A separate AAPI Data survey found 68% of Indian-American voters believe Trump has gone too far in restricting legal immigration.

The crackdown has also drawn fire from within the community's elected ranks. Representative Shri Thanedar, the Michigan Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee, criticized the PERM suspension on October 10, arguing the administration should target fraud, raise green-card caps and fund training for American tech workers instead of freezing the programme. The other side of the debate is not silent either: Vance's camp argues that years of programme abuse justify the crackdown, and the House bill's supporters say stiff fines are the only deterrent that works.

What's next

The immediate tests are legal, not electoral. Courts will decide whether the $100,000 fee survives its second injunction, and whether the PERM suspension for the eight named firms holds. For background on the fee's tangled history, see Trump Extends $100,000 H-1B Fee to September 2027 and US Green Card Freeze at Eight Tech Firms: What H-1B Workers Actually Face.

But the longer test arrives November 3. If Indian-American Republican candidates underperform in races they should be competitive in — while running on a party platform their own community's voters reject on immigration — the GOP's skilled-worker crackdown may prove to be an electoral own goal as much as an economic one. India's government has already warned that the green-card curbs "do not advance" the two countries' shared ambitions, a signal that the fallout is diplomatic as well as domestic.
